'''Levent Hasan Ali Alpöge''' (born April 1, 1992) is an American and Turkish [[mathematician]]. He is known for his work in [[number theory]] and [[statistics|arithmetic statistics]]. He was a Junior Fellow in the [[Harvard Society of Fellows]] and later joined the artificial-intelligence company [[Anthropic]] as a member of the technical staff.<ref name="cv">{{cite web |url=https://people.math.harvard.edu/~alpoge/cv.pdf |title=Curriculum Vitae |last=Alpöge |first=Levent |publisher=Harvard University Department of Mathematics |access-date=July 23, 2026}}</ref><ref name="conversation" /> In 2025, he and collaborators gave a second proof that [[Hilbert's tenth problem]] has a negative answer over the [[ring of integers]] of every [[algebraic number field]], a result originally established by Koymans and Pagano in 2024.<ref name="inventiones"/><ref name="Howlett2025">{{cite news
 |last=Howlett
 |first=Joseph
 |title=New Proofs Probe the Limits of Mathematical Truth
 |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/new-proofs-probe-the-limits-of-mathematical-truth-20250203/
 |work=Quanta Magazine
 |date=2025-02-03
}}</ref> 

On July 19, 2026, Alpöge presented an explicit [[counterexample]] to the [[Jacobian conjecture]] in three-dimensional space, stating that it was discovered using the [[Claude Mythos|Claude Fable 5]] AI model.<ref name="anthtweet">{{Cite tweet |user=__alpoge__ |number=2079028340955197566 |title=hello there the jacobian conjecture is false}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://fortune.com/2026/07/21/ai-solves-jacobian-conjecture-levant-alpoge-claude-fable-5/|title=Mathematicians grapple with a ‘very rapid and very unsettling change’ as AI cracks yet another century-old problem|publisher=|date=July 21, 2026|author=Roytburg|first=Eva|access-date=2026-07-23|work=[[Fortune (magazine)|Fortune]]}}</ref> He announced a counterexample to the [[Carathéodory conjecture]] on August 19, 2026 using the model. Four days later, he announced a positive answer to [[Almost_complex_manifold|Hopf's problem]] concerning the existence of a complex structure on a 6-dimensional sphere using AI tools.<ref name="AlpogeHopf2026">{{cite web |author=Levent Alpöge |title= The (3, 4, ∞) modular family of 2-tori, completed at its three special points, is a complex structure on S^6|date=24 August 2026 |url=https://alpo.ge/s6.pdf|access-date=26 August 2026
}}</ref>

His work on [[Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness]] with Tristan Buckmaster<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Howlett |first=Joseph |title=AI may have just solved a million-dollar math problem. The field will never be the same |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/ai-may-have-just-solved-a-million-dollar-math-problem-the-field-will-never-be-the-same/ |access-date=2026-09-08 |website=Scientific American |language=en}}</ref> was cited by [[OpenAI]] in their solution to the [[Millennium Prize Problems|Millennium Prize Problem]] on September 8, 2026.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news |last=Metz |first=Cade |date=2026-09-08 |title=OpenAI Says It Has Cracked One of Math’s ‘Millennium Problems’ |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/08/science/openai-proof-millennium-problem.html |access-date=2026-09-08 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-09-06 |title=On the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem |url=https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/ |access-date=2026-09-08 |website=OpenAI |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
[[File:Levent Alpöge 2018 MFO.jpg|thumb|Levent Alpöge in 2018]]
Alpöge was born on April 1, 1992, and grew up on [[Long Island]], New York, where he attended [[Half Hollow Hills Central School District|Half Hollow Hills High School West]] in [[Dix Hills, New York]].<ref name="cv"/><ref name="maviboncuk">{{cite web |url=http://maviboncuk.blogspot.com/2010/03/levent-alpoge-intel-science-talent.html |title=Levent Alpoge {{!}} Intel Science Talent Search 2010 Finalist |work=Mavi Boncuk |date=March 21, 2010 |access-date=July 23, 2026}}</ref> He holds dual United States and Turkish citizenship.<ref name="cv"/> 

In 2010, he was a finalist in the [[Regeneron Science Talent Search|Intel Science Talent Search]] for a computer-science project on the algorithmic analysis of [[magnetic resonance imaging|MRI]] scans of blood vessels. His earliest publication, on a [[CUDA]]-optimized vessel-detection method, dates from the same period.<ref name="maviboncuk" /><ref name="cv" /> He earned a [[Barry Goldwater Scholarship and Excellence in Education Foundation|Barry Goldwater Scholarship]].<ref name="cv" /><ref name="churchill" /> The [[Asteroid belt|main-belt asteroid]] 25898 Alpöge is named after him.<ref name="jpl">{{cite web |url=https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/tools/sbdb_lookup.html#/?sstr=20025898 |title=25898 Alpoge |work=JPL Small-Body Database |publisher=[[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]] |access-date=July 23, 2026}}</ref>

Alpöge studied at [[Harvard University]], where he received a Bachelor of Arts in mathematics and a Master of Arts in physics in 2014, graduating [[summa cum laude]].<ref name="cv" /> His undergraduate thesis, ''The average elliptic curve has few integral points'', was supervised by [[Jacob Tsimerman]].<ref name="cv" /><ref name="churchill">{{cite web |url=https://www.chu.cam.ac.uk/news/people/churchill-student-receives-prestigious-morgan-priz/ |title=Churchill student receives prestigious Morgan Prize for Outstanding Research in Mathematics |publisher=[[Churchill College, Cambridge]] |access-date=July 23, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/openai-jacob-tsimerman-fields-medal-ai-safety-391d0f79|title=The Math Superstar Who’s Terrified of AI—and Just Took a Job at OpenAI|first=Ben|last=Cohen|date=August 1, 2026|via=www.wsj.com}}</ref> 

After earning a graduate fellowship from the [[National Science Foundation]], Alpöge studied Part III of the [[Mathematical Tripos]] at the [[University of Cambridge]] as a [[Churchill Scholarship|Churchill Scholar]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kacoyanis |first=Stephanie |date=2014-04-15 |title=Senior wins Churchill Scholarship |url=https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2014/04/senior-wins-churchill-scholarship/ |access-date=2026-07-24 |website=Harvard Gazette |language=en-US}}</ref> earning a [[Master of Advanced Studies]] degree in 2015.<ref name="churchill" /><ref name="eurekalert" /> He received his [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] from [[Princeton University]] in 2020 with a dissertation titled ''Points on Curves'', supervised by [[Manjul Bhargava]].<ref name="cv" />

== Career ==
After completing his doctorate, Alpöge held an [[National Science Foundation|NSF]] Postdoctoral Fellowship affiliated with [[Columbia University]] and Harvard from 2020, and was a Junior Fellow in the [[Harvard Society of Fellows]] from 2021 to 2025.<ref name="cv"/><ref name="quanta2022"/> He subsequently joined the artificial-intelligence company [[Anthropic]] as a member of the technical staff.<ref name="conversation"/>

== Research ==
Alpöge works in number theory and arithmetic statistics, including the study of [[rational point|rational]] and integral points on [[Elliptic curve|elliptic]] and higher-genus curves, [[Selmer group]]s, and the distribution of arithmetic invariants of number fields.<ref name="cv"/>

=== Sums of two rational cubes ===
With [[Manjul Bhargava]] and Ari Shnidman, Alpöge established the first proven bounds on the proportion of integers that can be written as a sum of two [[Cube (algebra)|cubes]] of [[rational number]]s. Their 2022 work showed that at most about five-sixths of integers are so expressible, combining [[geometry of numbers]] techniques with the [[Hardy–Littlewood circle method|circle method]].<ref name="quanta2022">{{cite web |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/mathematical-trio-advances-centuries-old-number-theory-problem-20221129/ |title=Mathematical Trio Advances Centuries-Old Number Theory Problem |last=Cepelewicz |first=Jordana |work=[[Quanta Magazine]] |date=November 29, 2022 |access-date=July 23, 2026}}</ref> The upper bound for the density of integers that are so expressible has been subsequently improved to 68.05% by Peter Koymans and Alexander Smith. <ref>{{cite arxiv
 |last1=Koymans
 |first1=Peter
 |last2=Smith
 |first2=Alexander
 |title=Sums of rational cubes and the 3-Selmer group
 |eprint=2405.09311
 |class=math.NT
 |year=2024
}} Corollary 1.7.</ref>

=== Hilbert's tenth problem over number fields ===
In a paper published in ''[[Inventiones Mathematicae]]'' in 2025, Alpöge, Bhargava, [[Wei Ho (mathematician)|Wei Ho]], and Ari Shnidman proved that for any [[quadratic extension]] of number fields <math>K/F</math> there exists an [[abelian variety]] over <math>F</math> of positive [[Rank of an abelian group|rank]] whose rank does not grow after [[base change map|base change]] to <math>K</math>. This implies that [[Hilbert's tenth problem]] has a negative solution over the [[ring of integers]] of every algebraic number field—that is, there is no [[algorithm]] to decide whether a polynomial equation has solutions in that ring.<ref name="inventiones">{{cite journal |last1=Alpöge |first1=Levent |last2=Bhargava |first2=Manjul |last3=Ho |first3=Wei |last4=Shnidman |first4=Ari |title=Rank stability in quadratic extensions and Hilbert's tenth problem for the ring of integers of a number field |journal=[[Inventiones Mathematicae]] |volume=243 |pages=1129–1139 |year=2026 |doi=10.1007/s00222-025-01392-3 |arxiv=2501.18774}}</ref> The result gave an alternative completion of a program relating Hilbert's tenth problem to the rank stability of elliptic curves and abelian varieties initiated by [[Bjorn Poonen]], [[Barry Mazur]], [[Karl Rubin]], and Alexandra Shlapentokh; the Mazur--Rubin-Poonen-Shlapentokh program had been completed in 2024 by Peter Koymans and Carlo Pagano, using instead elliptic curves. <ref name="Howlett2025"/><ref>{{cite arxiv
 |last1=Koymans
 |first1=Peter
 |last2=Pagano
 |first2=Carlo
 |title=Hilbert's tenth problem via additive combinatorics
 |eprint=2412.01768
 |class=math.NT
 |year=2024
}}</ref>

=== Jacobian conjecture counterexample ===
In July 2026, Alpöge announced on the social-media platform [[X (social network)|X]] that, using Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 [[large language model]], he had found a counterexample to the [[Jacobian conjecture]], a problem in [[algebraic geometry]] begun by [[Ludwig Kraus]] in 1884 and formally posed by [[Ott-Heinrich Keller]] in 1939.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Burgess |first=Kaya |date=July 21, 2026 |title=Harvard mathematician uses AI to crack 87-year-old riddle |url=https://www.thetimes.com/uk/technology-uk/article/harvard-mathematician-uses-ai-to-crack-87-year-old-riddle-2s589kt5r |work=The Times}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Sparkes |first=Matthew |date=2026-07-20 |title=AI's solution to 87-year-old riddle takes mathematicians by surprise {{!}} New Scientist |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/2580374-ais-solution-to-87-year-old-riddle-takes-mathematicians-by-surprise/ |access-date=2026-07-24 |work=New Scientist |language=en-GB}}</ref> The example is a [[polynomial]] map from three-dimensional [[complex number|complex]] space to itself whose [[Jacobian determinant]] is the nonzero constant −2 but which is not injective, disproving the conjecture in dimensions three and above. The two-variable case of the conjecture remains open. The announcement was made outside of formal [[peer review]], and the arithmetic of the example was independently checked by other mathematicians in the days that followed.<ref name="conversation">{{cite web |url=https://theconversation.com/hello-there-the-jacobian-conjecture-is-false-thanx-why-a-tiny-social-media-post-has-mathematicians-rethinking-ai-283883 |title='hello there the jacobian conjecture is false thanx': why a tiny social media post has mathematicians rethinking AI |work=[[The Conversation (website)|The Conversation]] |date=July 2026 |access-date=July 23, 2026}}</ref>

===Hadamard matrices===
On August 12, 2026, Alpöge announced on X that, together with Philippe Voinov and Saul Reynolds-Haertle and using Anthropic's Claude, he had constructed [[Hadamard matrix|Hadamard matrices]] for all twelve orders below 2000 for which no such matrix had previously been known: 668, 716, 892, 1132, 1244, 1388, 1436, 1676, 1772, 1916, 1948 and 1964.<ref name="mathworld-hadamard">{{cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=Hadamard Matrix |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/HadamardMatrix.html |website=MathWorld |access-date=September 10, 2026}}</ref><ref name="epoch-hadamard">{{cite web |title=Hadamard Matrix of Order 668 |url=https://epoch.ai/frontiermath/open-problems/hadamard |website=Epoch AI |access-date=September 10, 2026}}</ref> Order 668 had been the smallest open case of the [[Hadamard matrix#Hadamard conjecture|Hadamard conjecture]] since 2005.<ref name="mathworld-hadamard" />

===Carathéodory conjecture counterexample===
On August 19, 2026, he announced an explicit <math> C^\infty </math> counterexample for the [[Carathéodory conjecture]] checked with John-Paul Smith and Anthropic's artificial-intelligence system Claude.<ref name="AlpogeCaratheodory2026">{{cite tweet |user=__alpoge__ |author=Levent Alpöge |number=2089971359921156203 |title=a week ago i chatted with @AchimWar about favourite problems and the caratheodory conjecture came up |date=19 August 2026 |access-date=26 August 2026
}}</ref> Once again the result was announced in a tweet<ref>{{Cite news |date=2026-08-19 |title=levent (@__alpoge__) on X |url=https://x.com/__alpoge__/status/2089971359921156203 |access-date=2026-09-08 |work=X (formerly Twitter) |language=en-US}}</ref>, but on this occasion Alpoge offered a more comprehensive backstory, asserting that "i literally wanted to just read about it but i did see the complicated literature situation and so in hopes i could help asked him if it was ok to look at with a model" before confirming that "i did wanna have it recorded somewhere public though" and then giving the example.

===Hopf's problem===
Alpöge announced an answer to [[Almost_complex_manifold|Hopf's problem]] on X on August 23, 2026, stating that he constructed a [[complex manifold]] structure on a [[N-sphere|6-dimensional sphere]] using one of Anthropic's models.<ref>https://x.com/alpoge/status/2091639597193368014</ref><ref name="AlpogeHopf2026">{{cite web |author=Levent Alpöge |title= The (3, 4, ∞) modular family of 2-tori, completed at its three special points, is a complex structure on S^6|date=24 August 2026 |url=https://alpo.ge/s6.pdf|access-date=26 August 2026
}}</ref> The same day Alpöge published a 100-page document containing a proof of the positive solution on his personal website.<ref>https://alpo.ge/s6.pdf</ref>. 

Proposed formalizations by Dean Cureton<ref>https://github.com/deancureton/sphere-six-complex</ref> and by Boris Alexeev<ref>https://github.com/plby/HopfProblem</ref> were subsequently posted on [[GitHub]], and Philip Engel published some notes about the proof.<ref>https://philip-engel.github.io/S6.pdf</ref> {{ill|Manon Bischoff|de}} reported on the finding in ''Spektrum der Wissenschaft'', the German language edition of ''[[Scientific American]]''.<ref>[https://www.spektrum.de/news/ki-loest-hopf-vermutung-zu-sechsdimensionalen-kugeln/2341467 KI löst angeblich jahrzehntealtes Problem zu sechsdimensionalen Kugeln] (AI allegedly solves decades-old problem about 6-dimensional spheres), spektrum.de, 28 August 2026.</ref>

===Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness===
{{Main|Navier–Stokes priority controversy}}
Alpöge worked with [[New York University]] mathematician {{ill|Tristan Buckmaster|de}} on the [[Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness]] problem, one of the seven [[Millennium Prize Problems]]. On August 15, 2026, the pair proved that the [[Euler equations (fluid dynamics)|Euler equations]], the frictionless counterpart of Navier–Stokes, can "blow up" in finite time, extending a forcing technique developed by {{ill|Diego Córdoba|eu|Diego Córdoba Gazolaz}} and {{ill|Luis Martínez-Zoroa|eu|Luis Martínez Zoroa}}.<ref name=":0" /> After verifying the proof in [[Lean (proof assistant)|Lean]], the pair published a preprint establishing finite-time blow-up with smooth forcing for the incompressible porous medium equation, the 2D Boussinesq system, and the 3D incompressible Euler equations, using Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's [[OpenAI Codex (AI agent)|Codex]] in the work.<ref name=":0" />

After word of the pair's progress reached OpenAI, a team led by OpenAI scientist [[Sébastien Bubeck]] used an internal model to find a solution for Navier–Stokes equations.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-09-08 |title=OpenAI says it cracked 90-year-old maths problem in 88 hours |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cy7zygy3rl2o |access-date=2026-09-08 |website=www.bbc.com |language=en-GB}}</ref> On September 8, 2026, OpenAI announced a full solution to the problem that resembled the approach used by the pair.<ref name=":1" /> Buckmaster suggested OpenAI researchers may have accessed private work he had stored in a Codex session before publication.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=A Mathematician Working On The Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem Now Wonders If OpenAI Stole His Notes That He Stored In Codex |url=https://wccftech.com/a-mathematician-working-on-the-navier-stokes-millennium-prize-problem-now-wonders-if-openai-stole-his-notes-that-he-stored-in-codex/ |website=WCCFTech}}</ref><!--As of September 8, 2026, the Clay Mathematics Institute still listed Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness as unsolved--><ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Mills |first=Madison |date=2026-09-08 |title=OpenAI's historic math solution overshadowed by credit controversy |url=https://www.axios.com/2026/09/08/openai-math-solution-navier-stokes-credit |access-date=2026-09-08 |website=Axios |language=en}}</ref>
